questions.e: The chair has no angle strain and fully staggered bonds.

questions.q: The A-value of a methyl group (axial–equatorial free energy difference) is about:
questions.e: Methyl: about 1.7–1.8 kcal/mol; tert-butyl is more than 4.5.

questions.q: The most stable chair of trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane has:
c: The ring in a boat form
questions.e: For trans-1,4 the two chairs are diequatorial or diaxial; diequatorial is much lower in energy.

questions.q: Why does a tert-butyl group effectively lock a cyclohexane ring in one chair, and how can this be used mechanistically?
questions.m: Axial tert-butyl suffers severe 1,3-diaxial interactions (A-value ≳ 4.5–5 kcal/mol), so >99.9% of molecules at room temperature place it equatorial. A tert-butyl substituent can then be used as a conformational anchor to study the reactivity of axial versus equatorial groups at other positions (e.g., E2 requiring axial leaving groups).

questions.e: Replacing each H in turn gives enantiomers, and a mirror plane (but no C₂) interconverts them.

questions.q: The two hydrogens of CH₂Cl₂ are:

questions.q: Define diastereotopic protons and say how they appear in the ¹H NMR of a chiral molecule such as 2-butanol.
questions.m: Diastereotopic protons (e.g., the CH₂ protons next to a stereocenter) give diastereomeric products on replacement; they are chemically inequivalent even in an achiral solvent and can show distinct chemical shifts and couple to each other (geminal J), producing complex patterns. Enantiotopic protons are equivalent in achiral media.

questions.q: Classical resolution of a racemic amine with enantiopure tartaric acid works because it:
c: Forms diastereomeric salts with different solubilities
Forms enantiomeric salts with different solubilities
Converts one enantiomer to the other
questions.e: Diastereomers have different physical properties and can be separated by crystallization.

questions.q: A mixture is 75% R and 25% S. Its enantiomeric excess is:
A sample shows [α] = +30° while the pure enantiomer has [α] = +60°. The optical purity (≈ ee) is:
What is the maximum yield of a single enantiomer in a classic kinetic resolution, and how can dynamic kinetic resolution exceed it?
questions.m: A classical kinetic resolution can give at most 50% of the unreacted enantiomer (or 50% of the product, in theory) since the other enantiomer is consumed or discarded. In dynamic kinetic resolution the substrate enantiomers rapidly interconvert (racemize) under the reaction conditions, so the faster-reacting enantiomer is continually replenished and up to 100% yield of a single stereoisomer is possible.

questions.q: The Felkin–Anh model predicts nucleophilic attack on an α-chiral carbonyl occurs:
c: Anti to the largest α-substituent, along the Bürgi–Dunitz trajectory
Perpendicular to the carbonyl plane through the O
questions.e: The largest group sits perpendicular to the C=O plane and the nucleophile approaches near 107° to C=O, anti to it.
